title: Translation into orbit-functor automorphisms is a topological embedding
statement: Let $G$ be a Hausdorff topological group whose identity has a basis of open subgroups. Let $\mathcal O_G$, $i_G$, $\omega_G$ and $F_G$ be the open-orbit category, its inclusion into discrete continuous left $G$-sets, and the two underlying-set functors [def-sfb-open-orbit-functor]. Give natural automorphism groups the pointwise topology [def-sfb-set-functor-aut-pointwise-topology]. Work in compatible universes. The open subgroups and the equivariant maps between their coset sets form a small category, and a natural automorphism of $\omega_G$ is precisely a family of bijections $\alpha_U:G/U\to G/U$ commuting with all equivariant maps. The family $\Phi(g)_U(x)=gx$ defines a group homomorphism $\Phi:G\to\operatorname{Aut}(\omega_G)$. The pointwise topology makes $\operatorname{Aut}(\omega_G)$ a topological group, and $\Phi$ is an injective topological embedding (the topology of $G$ is induced by $\Phi$). For $x=aU$, its stabilizer is $aUa^{-1}$ and every fibre of $g\mapsto gx$ is a clopen left coset of that subgroup. For every open subgroup $U$, $\Phi^{-1}(\{\alpha:\alpha_U(U)=U\})=U$.

source.place: Proposition 7.1.5, printed p. 64, natural map and injectivity; returned item proof steps 1–3.

proof.text: Smallness: the open subgroups form a subset of the power set of $G$. For each pair $U,V$, the equivariant maps form a subset of the set of functions $G/U\to G/V$. Thus the objects and all arrows form sets in compatible universes. Identities and composition are those of functions, as in [def-sfb-open-orbit-functor].

source.place: Section 7.1, Proposition 7.1.5, printed pp. 63–64; explicit elementary verification of the natural translation map, step 1

proof.text: Unpack natural automorphisms using [def-sfb-open-orbit-functor]: their components are bijections $\alpha_U:G/U\to G/U$ satisfying $f\alpha_U=\alpha_Vf$ for every equivariant $f:G/U\to G/V$. Conversely such a family is natural, and its inverses are natural since this equality gives $f\alpha_U^{-1}=\alpha_V^{-1}f$. Hence it is a natural automorphism. Multiplication is componentwise composition: $(\alpha\beta)_U(x)=\alpha_U(\beta_U(x))$.

source.place: Section 7.1, Proposition 7.1.5, printed pp. 63–64; explicit elementary verification of the natural translation map, step 2

proof.text: Translation by $g$ on each coset set has inverse translation by $g^{-1}$. For every equivariant $f$ one has $f(gx)=g f(x)$, so these bijections define $\Phi(g)$. The action identities give $\Phi(1)_U(x)=x$ and $\Phi(gh)_U(x)=g(hx)=(\Phi(g)\Phi(h))_U(x)$ for every $U,x$; equality of components proves that $\Phi$ is a homomorphism.

source.place: Section 7.1, Proposition 7.1.5, printed pp. 63–64; explicit elementary verification of the natural translation map, step 3

proof.text: For the topology of [def-sfb-set-functor-aut-pointwise-topology], verify multiplication at a pair $(\alpha,\beta)$ one coordinate $(U,x)$ at a time. The open conditions $\beta'_U(x)=\beta_U(x)$ and $\alpha'_U(\beta_U(x))=\alpha_U(\beta_U(x))$ imply $(\alpha'\beta')_U(x)=(\alpha\beta)_U(x)$. Intersect these conditions for the finitely many coordinates in any basic neighbourhood. These product neighbourhoods prove joint continuity of multiplication.

source.place: Section 7.1, Proposition 7.1.5, printed pp. 63–64; explicit elementary verification of the natural translation map, step 4

proof.text: For inversion at $\alpha$, fix a coordinate $(U,x)$ and put $y=\alpha_U^{-1}(x)$. The open condition $\alpha'_U(y)=x=\alpha_U(y)$ forces $(\alpha'_U)^{-1}(x)=y$, because $\alpha'_U$ is bijective. Intersect for finitely many coordinates, using the basis in [def-sfb-set-functor-aut-pointwise-topology]. This proves continuity of inversion, so the natural automorphism group is a topological group.

source.place: Section 7.1, Proposition 7.1.5, printed pp. 63–64; explicit elementary verification of the natural translation map, step 5

proof.text: For $x=aU$, the equality $hx=x$ is equivalent to $a^{-1}ha\in U$, so its stabilizer is $H=aUa^{-1}$. Conjugation and left translation are homeomorphisms: their formulas and inverse formulas are compositions of continuous multiplication and inversion. Thus $H$ and each left coset of $H$ are open. The complement of $H$ is the union of its other left cosets, so $H$ and all its translates are also closed. Every value $bU$ of $g\mapsto gx$ is attained, for example by $g_0=ba^{-1}$, and its fibre is exactly $g_0H$, since $gx=g_0x$ iff $g_0^{-1}g\in H$.

source.place: Section 7.1, Proposition 7.1.5, printed pp. 63–64; explicit elementary verification of the natural translation map, step 6

proof.text: The inverse image under $\Phi$ of a condition $\alpha_U(x)=z$ is the clopen fibre just computed. Finite intersections of these conditions are a basis by [def-sfb-set-functor-aut-pointwise-topology], so $\Phi$ is continuous. At the identity coset, $\Phi(g)_U(U)=U$ iff $gU=U$ iff $g\in U$. Hence $\Phi^{-1}(\{\alpha:\alpha_U(U)=U\})=U$ for every open subgroup $U$.

source.place: Section 7.1, Proposition 7.1.5, printed pp. 63–64; explicit elementary verification of the natural translation map, step 7

proof.text: For any $g\in G$ and open subgroup $U$, the coordinate-open set $E_{g,U}=\{\alpha:\alpha_U(U)=gU\}$ has inverse image $gU$. These translates form a basis of the original topology: if $g\in O$ with $O$ open, choose an open subgroup $U\subseteq g^{-1}O$, giving $gU\subseteq O$. Consequently the topology induced by $\Phi$ contains every original open set. Continuity proved above gives the opposite containment. Together with injectivity, equality of these topologies is precisely the asserted topological embedding.
